setup.zh: 开春，舅舅从县城来，念了一张告示：沉鼎观开山门，录为弟子者，家里每年五两银子。他刚念到「沉鼎」，你胸口的木牌烫得像一块炭。
setup.en: In spring Uncle comes from the county town and reads out a notice: Chending Temple opens its gate, and a disciple's family gets five taels a year. At the words "Chending" the token at your chest burns like a coal.

recap.zh: 舅舅带来了沉鼎观开山门的告示；他念到「沉鼎」，木牌烫得像炭——你决定去。
recap.en: Uncle brought the notice that Chending Temple would open its gate; at "Chending" the token burned like a coal — and you decided to go.

zh: 舅舅：簇新的青布长衫，二斤肉，一包红糖。
en: Uncle: a brand-new blue gown, two jin of meat, a packet of brown sugar.
"…present themselves for trial at the foot of Chending Mountain."
Between your fingers, a thread of silver light.

story.zh:
三月初三，上巳，舅舅来了。舅舅是小满他娘的亲弟弟，在县城济世堂做账房，是沈家这一门亲戚里唯一「出息了」的人。他穿一身簇新的青布长衫，提着二斤肉、一包红糖，站在那扇装歪了的门口，拿袖子掩着鼻子，咳了一声。

他爹慌慌张张地拿袖子擦炕沿，擦了三遍，才请他坐。舅舅坐是坐下了，屁股只沾了半边。他看了看屋顶，看了看墙角接水的那一排盆——十七个，整整齐齐，像一队站岗的兵——又看了看姐夫的膝盖，叹了口气：「姐，你这日子……」小满他娘道：「挺好。」「屋顶都漏成这样了——」「通风。」「这墙都裂了——」「透亮。」

舅舅张了张嘴，压低了声音：「姐，你当年要是听爹的话——」他娘道：「吃饭。」舅舅便闭上了嘴。小满心里一动：外公的话，是什么话？他看看他娘，她正低头给舅舅盛饭，盛得满满的；他爹低着头，一下一下地揉膝盖，揉得很用力。

吃饭的时候，舅舅从怀里摸出一张纸：「县城贴的告示。我给你们抄了一份。」清了清嗓子，念道：「**沉鼎观**，三年一开山门，收徒。凡十二至十六岁、身家清白者，皆可于九月初九，赴泗水沉鼎山下应试。录为弟子者，其家每岁由观中发给白银五两——」

他刚念到「沉鼎」两个字，小满胸口的木牌登时烫得像一块刚从灶膛里扒出来的炭，烫得他「嗷——！」的一声从凳子上蹦起来，一口饭，不偏不倚，全喷在了舅舅脸上。

舅舅坐在那儿，脸上挂着饭粒，一动不动。一粒米从他眉毛上慢慢滑下来，滑到鼻尖上，停了一停，才掉进他面前那碗饭里。小满捂着胸口道：「……噎、噎着了。」舅舅掏出帕子擦了脸，瞧了瞧碗里那粒米，终于还是把那碗饭端起来，吃了。济世堂的账房，是不糟蹋粮食的。

没有人看见，小满捂在胸口的手指缝里，漏出了一线银光。木牌上那条银色的尾巴，不再一明一暗了，它亮着，一直亮着，像一个在梦里找了很久很久的人，终于听见了自己要找的那个名字。

他娘问道：「五两银子？」「一年五两。」他爹放下了筷子。沈家一年交马家的租，加上山风钱，加上这个钱那个钱，也不过三两。舅舅又压低了声音：「还有。家里有孩子进了仙门的——马家，不敢收租。」屋里静了。隔了一会儿，舅舅道：「姐。二十年前，我也去过。」

「那年我十四。三百级石阶，要在一炷香里走完。我爬到一百六十级，腿就动不了了。我在那儿坐了一炷香，看着别人一个一个从我身边走过去。然后我就下山了，去济世堂学打算盘。」他说这话的时候，眼睛看着桌上那碗饭，声音平得像在念账本上的一行字。小满他娘轻轻地道：「上回你说是一百五十级。」「……一百六十级。」「上上回，一百四十。」

舅舅的脸登时红得跟他提来的那二斤肉一个颜色：「每年都在长嘛！人老了，记性好了！」他爹在旁边很真诚地道：「那再过几年，您就爬上去了。」舅舅瞪了姐夫一眼。小满憋不住了，问道：「舅舅，你见过仙人吗？」舅舅的神色登时郑重起来：「见过。前年冬天，济世堂来过一个穿灰袍的，走路没声儿，买了三两当归，给了块碎银子。我要找他钱，他摆摆手：不必。」舅舅学着摆了摆手，「坐了十八年柜台，头一回有人跟我说不必。」小满心想：走路没声儿的人，买当归做什么？舅舅已经转过头来，看着他：「你娘识字，你随她，脑子比我活。你爹打猎，你随他，腿脚比我稳。去试试。进不去，也不亏什么。进去了——」他没说完，看了一眼姐夫的膝盖，又看了一眼墙角那一排盆，便低下头吃饭了。
story.en:
On the third of the third month, the Shangsi festival, his uncle came. His uncle was his mother's own younger brother, bookkeeper at the Jishi Hall in the county town, the one relative in the Shen family who had "made something of himself". He wore a brand-new blue cloth gown and carried two catties of meat and a packet of brown sugar, and stood at the crooked door, sleeve over his nose, and coughed.

Xiaoman's father hurriedly wiped the edge of the kang with his sleeve three times before asking him to sit. His uncle sat — but only half his backside touched. He looked at the roof, at the row of basins in the corner catching drips — seventeen, lined up neat as a squad of sentries — at his brother-in-law's knee, and sighed. "Sister, this life of yours…" Xiaoman's mother said, "It's fine." "The roof's leaking like this —" "Ventilation." "The walls are cracked —" "Lets the light in."

His uncle opened his mouth and lowered his voice. "Sister, if you'd listened to Father back then —" His mother said, "Eat." His uncle shut his mouth. Xiaoman was struck: Grandfather's words — what words? He looked at his mother; she had her head down, dishing rice for his uncle, piling the bowl high; his father had his head down too, rubbing his knee over and over, very hard.

Over the meal his uncle took a sheet of paper from his coat. "A notice posted in the county town. I copied it out for you." He cleared his throat and read: "**Chending Temple** opens its mountain gate once every three years to take disciples. All between twelve and sixteen years of age, of clean family, may present themselves for trial at the foot of Chending Mountain on the Si River on the ninth day of the ninth month. For those enrolled as disciples, the Temple will grant their family five taels of silver each year —"

The moment he read the word *Chending*, the token at Xiaoman's chest burned like a coal just raked from the stove, so hot that Xiaoman leapt off his stool with a yelp — and a mouthful of rice went, squarely, all over his uncle's face.

His uncle sat there with rice on his face, perfectly still. One grain slid slowly down from his eyebrow to the tip of his nose, paused, and dropped into the bowl in front of him. Xiaoman clutched his chest. "…I ch-choked." His uncle took out a handkerchief and wiped his face, looked at the grain in his bowl, and in the end picked up the bowl and ate it. The bookkeeper of the Jishi Hall does not waste grain.

Nobody saw the thread of silver light leaking between the fingers Xiaoman pressed to his chest. The silver tail on the token no longer went bright and dim; it was lit and stayed lit, like someone who has searched a long, long time in a dream and at last heard the very name they were looking for.

His mother asked, "Five taels of silver?" "Five taels a year." His father put down his chopsticks. The Shens' rent to the Mas, plus the mountain-wind money, plus this money and that, came to no more than three taels a year. His uncle lowered his voice again. "And. A family with a child who's got into an immortal sect — the Mas daren't take rent from them." The room went quiet. After a while his uncle said, "Sister. Twenty years ago, I went too."

"I was fourteen. Three hundred stone steps, to be climbed within one stick of incense. I got to step one hundred and sixty, and my legs wouldn't move. I sat there the length of a stick of incense, watching others walk past me one by one. Then I came down the mountain and went to the Jishi Hall to learn the abacus." As he said it his eyes were on the bowl of rice, his voice flat as reading out a line of a ledger. Xiaoman's mother said softly, "Last time you said a hundred and fifty." "…A hundred and sixty." "The time before, a hundred and forty."

His uncle's face went red as the two catties of meat he'd brought. "It grows every year! Getting older, my memory's getting better!" Xiaoman's father said, quite sincerely, "Then in a few more years you'll have got to the top." His uncle glared at his brother-in-law. Xiaoman couldn't hold it in: "Uncle, have you ever seen an immortal?" His uncle's face turned solemn at once. "I have. The winter before last a man in a grey robe came into the Jishi Hall, walked without a sound, bought three ounces of angelica root and paid with a piece of broken silver. I went to give him change; he waved a hand: *No need.*" His uncle waved a hand the same way. "Eighteen years at that counter, and the first time anyone ever said *no need* to me." Xiaoman thought: what would a man who walks without a sound want with angelica root? His uncle had already turned to look at him. "Your mother can read — you take after her, a quicker head than mine. Your father hunts — you take after him, steadier legs than mine. Go and try. If you don't get in, you've lost nothing. If you do —" He didn't finish; he looked at his brother-in-law's knee, at the row of basins in the corner, and lowered his head and ate.

exits.means: decides to go to the temple trials

story.zh:
那天夜里，小满躺在炕上，一直睁着眼睛。他在心里算账，像他娘教他的那样，一笔一笔地算。五两银子，一年。他爹，再也不用拖着那条腿进深山；他娘，下雨天再也不用把家里十七个盆都摆出来；马三的短棍，再也敲不到沈家的门框；那件棉袄，今年冬天便有了，袖子不短，手腕不冻。然后，是另一笔账。

他把木牌从衣领里掏出来，贴在耳朵边上听。什么都听不见，可它亮着。那条银色的尾巴，从晌午舅舅念告示的时候亮起来，一直亮到这时候，一刻也没暗过。「……本王在找一个地方……一个名字……等你听见了，本王会知道的。」他听见了。她也知道了。他对着黑暗，小声说道：「好。我去。」木牌暖了一下。

这一夜的数，他娘记在「红糖一包，舅舅给」底下：

三月初三。满，五十六，毛飞。离九月初九，一百八十四日。

舅舅是第二天一早走的。走出村口半里地，路边草垛后头钻出一个红鼻头的小姑娘，冲他鞠了一躬：「舅舅好。」舅舅吓了一跳：「我不是你舅舅。」「你是小满的舅舅。小满的舅舅，就是舅舅。」舅舅觉得这话有几分道理。小姑娘只问了一句：「考仙门，考不考算账？」舅舅上下打量了她一番，又问了她几句，她答得又快又清楚。舅舅便笑了，从怀里摸出一本济世堂用剩的空账簿，巴掌大小，蓝布面儿，递给了她。这件事，小满不知道。

舅舅走了的那天夜里，他娘把竹简翻到了最后一片。她说，这是卷末，前头教怎么走，这里说路在哪里。那一片上只有一行：「而有百日筑基，十月胎圆，三年乳哺之功之验。」

「筑基……」他娘念到这两个字，手指停住了，「筑什么基？盖房子？」她又往下念：「十月胎圆，三年乳哺——这倒像是生孩子。」她说着笑了一下。那笑还没收住，她的手指又回到了「筑基」两个字上，停着，停了很久。

小满问：「娘，怎么了？」

「没什么。」她把竹简卷上了。过了一会儿，她道：「你舅舅说的那句话——你外公的话。你外公说，人这一辈子，得往上走。我说，往上走的人够多了，山脚下总得有人把灶烧着。」她吹灭了灯。

小满在黑地里掰着指头算：百日筑基，一百天。离九月初九，一百八十三日。够筑一回，还富余八十三天。他心里一宽，翻身睡了。这笔账，他算错了。错在哪里，他要到泗水边上，才会知道。

四月里，小满那一日刚过——他就是那一日生的，他娘那天多烙了一张饼，便算过了生日——春雨一连下了半个月，他爹的膝盖肿得像个发面馒头。他娘把攒下的一冬的兔皮卷成一卷，叫爷儿俩进城，卖了皮子，顺路去济世堂，叫舅舅求坐堂的先生瞧一瞧。

坐堂的是个瘦老郎中，一把山羊胡，三根指头搭在他爹腕子上，搭了半天，道：「膝盖是老伤，脉倒不坏。」舅舅在一旁陪着笑，见缝插针，便要显一显自己：「先生，我外甥要去考仙门，我也教他一手。吐纳嘛，我懂，存钱一个道理，多进少出——」说着便张大了嘴，一口接一口往里猛吸，吸了二十来口，吸得脸都白了，身子一晃，一屁股坐在了药碾子上，两只手直甩：「……麻、麻了。」

老郎中看都不看他，道：「二十年账房，一口气都喘在嗓子眼里。吸得那么猛，吐得那么急，身子里那点浊气，叫你吐得一干二净——浊气也是要留一点的，留得太少，人一样发晕，指头一样发麻。坐着，少说话，慢慢喘，一会儿就好。」舅舅坐在药碾子上，慢慢喘，果然一会儿就好了，脸却红了好一阵。

老郎中顺手把小满的腕子也拉了过去，一搭，眉毛一挑：「这孩子的脉，跳得倒慢，跟个挑了一辈子担的老挑夫似的。练过什么？」小满心里一紧，道：「挑水。」老郎中「嗯」了一声，指头没松，道：「你吸一口，再吐一口。」小满照做。老郎中道：「吸的时候，脉快了；吐的时候，脉慢了。人人都是这样，只是你这一快一慢，比旁人分得清楚。」

他这才松了手，捻着胡子道：「你舅舅说的，错了一半。肺管出气，肾管纳气——吸进来的气，光到胸口不算数，得一直沉到底下，腰眼那里，才算收进来了。呼出心与肺，吸入肾与肝，医书上的话。气浮在上头的人，一喘就喘；沉到底的人，挑一天的担也不喘。」他瞧了瞧小满，又瞧了瞧舅舅，「你外甥，比你会喘。」

回去的路，是一路上坡。他爹拄着棍走在前头，走一阵，回头看看儿子，道：「到了沉鼎山，石阶是一炷香三百级，你舅舅是一口气冲的。」他教小满：三步一吸，三步一呼，吸的时候气往下沉，呼的时候脚往前送；不看坡顶，只看脚底下这一级。「追兔子比快，追鹿比稳。山上的路，都是这么走完的。」

那天夜里，小满坐在柴垛上，学那句「吸入肾与肝」，把那口气往下送。他头一回觉出了一样东西：一缕热，随着那口气往下沉，沉过胸口，沉到肚脐，像一口热米汤咽下去，一路暖到底；到了肚脐底下，再往下，便没了，像往一口枯井里扔了一块石头，等了半天，听不见响。夜夜如此。他不知道那口井底下是什么，只知道他娘账本最末一页的「下」字，到如今还空着，没有画圈。

四月初九。满，六十七。毛翻。

说书的在这里多一句嘴：世上的拳师、挑夫、水手、猎户，把喘气练到这一步，也就到了头——一身的灶烧得旺，风箱拉得匀，力气比旁人足些，活得比旁人长些，如此而已。修仙的人，偏偏从这里起步。那口井，凡人的身子上是没有门的。

五月里青黄不接，老刘家的米缸见了底。老刘到马家借了两斗米，借据上按了个红手印，利钱三分。阿禾听说了，拿炭条在一个蓝布面的小本子上算了半天，算完了，看了刘豆芽一眼，没说话。

五月底，一连下了七天雨。墙角的盆，摆到了第十八个——第十八个，是他娘的洗脸盆。第七天夜里，炕头那边的屋顶漏开了一个口子，雨水顺着墙根灌进了炕洞。小满扑过去掏竹简，掏出来的时候，竹简在泥水里泡了半宿，绳子都胀了。他娘点了灯，把竹简一片一片摊在灶台上烘。烘到后半夜，她拿指头一片一片摸过去，摸到最后一片，抬起头来：「一个字也没花。」一卷山里捡来的竹简，绳子快烂了，竹片上还有虫蛀的眼儿，在泥水里泡了半宿，字一个也没花。他娘把它卷好，递给他，只说了一句：「换个地方藏。」

六月初，马家的管家胡四上老刘家讨那两斗米。借据上写的是秋后还，胡四拿指甲在「秋后」两个字上刮了一刮：「马家的秋，马家定。」老刘拿不出，胡四便换了个价钱：「沈家柴垛上闹的那个鬼，叫你家豆芽去瞧清楚。瞧清楚了，利钱减一半。」

刘豆芽不去柴垛，他去了河湾。那天晌午，村里的半大孩子都在河湾里扎猛子，刘豆芽当着一河的人，冲岸上的小满喊：「沈小满！你家柴垛上那个憋气的鬼，敢不敢下来，跟我比一比？谁在水底下待得久！」一河的孩子都起哄。小满知道，不下去，便是心虚。

两个人一齐扎进了那口深潭。小满往下一沉，先吐了半口气——一吐气，人便往下坠，像一块石头，一直沉到了潭底，盘腿坐在一块青石上。水底下很静，静得像他娘吹灭了灯的灶间，日头在头顶上碎成一片一片的金鳞。他忽然想笑：伸则下，原来是这么个下法。

在水底下憋不住，憋的人以为是清气用完了，其实不是——是身子里那座灶烧出来的烟攒满了，胸口一胀，催着人往上蹿。烟攒得慢，便待得久；烟攒得慢，靠的还是那颗心不慌。小满坐在潭底，心里数到了六十，那口气还稳稳的，像一盏掐短了灯芯的灯。他睁着眼睛，看见刘豆芽在旁边，腮帮子鼓着，一双眼睛瞪得溜圆，正瞪着他。

他想起了一个「藏」字，两脚一蹬，先蹿出了水面，呛着水，扒着岸边的石头直喘。过了好一会儿，刘豆芽才冒出头来。一河的孩子都嚷：「刘豆芽赢了！」

那天傍晚，刘豆芽在柴垛底下站住了，仰着脸，小声道：「我在底下看见了。你坐在那儿，跟块石头似的，眼睛还睁着。」小满没说话。刘豆芽又道：「我跟胡管家说，你憋不过我。」说完就走了。窗户里头，他娘的算盘「嗒」地响了一声，便没了动静。

胡四听了，笑了半天，利钱一文也没减。可这话传到马三耳朵里，马三没笑。他拿短棍敲着桌子想了一会儿，道：「憋气？县里开春贴了告示。沈家那小子，别是想去考仙门吧？」

那天夜里，账本最末一页的「下」字外头，画上了第四个圈。

六月十一。满，八十一。毛抖。

七月，数钉在八十九上，一钉二十来天，娘的账上行行都是「八十九」。有一夜他咬着牙硬往上顶，顶到九十一，那口气一炸，雁毛又飞了，第二天连八十九都数不到。他坐在柴垛上，第一回想：一百二十，也许本来就不是给凡人数的。
story.en:
That night Xiaoman lay on the kang with his eyes open. He did the accounts in his head, as his mother had taught him, item by item. Five taels of silver, a year. His father would never again have to drag that leg into the deep mountains; his mother would never again, on rainy days, set out all seventeen basins; Ma San's club would never again rap the Shens' doorframe; the coat would be there this winter, sleeves long enough, wrists not frozen. And then, the other account.

He took the token out from his collar and held it to his ear. He heard nothing, but it was lit. The silver tail had lit up at noon when his uncle read the notice, and stayed lit till now, not dimming for a moment. "…This king is looking for a place… a name… when you hear it, this king will know." He had heard it. And she knew. Into the dark he said softly: "All right. I'll go." The token warmed, once.

That night's count his mother entered under "Brown sugar, one packet, from Uncle":

Third month, third. Man: fifty-six, feather flew. To the ninth of the ninth month: one hundred and eighty-four days.

His uncle left early the next morning. Half a li beyond the village gate a red-nosed little girl popped out from behind a haystack by the road and bowed to him. "Hello, Uncle." His uncle jumped. "I'm not your uncle." "You're Xiaoman's uncle. Xiaoman's uncle is Uncle." His uncle felt there was some sense in that. The girl asked just one question: "The immortal-gate exam — does it test reckoning?" His uncle looked her up and down, asked her a few questions, and she answered them quick and clear. His uncle laughed, took from his coat an empty ledger left over from the Jishi Hall, palm-sized, blue cloth cover, and gave it to her. Xiaoman didn't know about this.

The night his uncle left, his mother turned the scroll to its last slip. This, she said, was the end: the earlier parts teach how to walk; this part says where the road is.

That slip had just one line: "*and so there came the proofs of a hundred days' foundation-building, ten months' round womb, three years' nursing.*"

"Foundation-building…" At those words his mother's finger stopped. "Building what foundation? A house?" She read on: "Ten months' round womb, three years' nursing — sounds like having a baby." She laughed a little as she said it. Before the laugh was gone her finger went back to *foundation-building* and stayed there, a long time.

Xiaoman asked, "Mum, what is it?"

"Nothing." She rolled up the scroll. After a while she said, "That thing your uncle said — your grandfather's words. Your grandfather said a person must go up in this life. I said plenty of people are going up; somebody at the foot of the mountain has to keep the stove lit." She blew out the lamp.

In the dark Xiaoman counted on his fingers: a hundred days' foundation-building, a hundred days. To the ninth of the ninth month, a hundred and eighty-three days. Enough to build one, with eighty-three days to spare. His heart eased; he rolled over and slept.

He'd reckoned that account wrong. Where he'd gone wrong he wouldn't learn until he reached the bank of the Si River.

In the fourth month, just after Xiaoman day — he'd been born on that day, and his mother made one extra flatbread that day and that was his birthday — his father shouldered the hoe for the slope field and told him to come. The slope field was halfway up the mountain, a steep slope cut with dozens of stone steps, high and low, some that wobbled when you stepped on them. Xiaoman ran up two and three at a time and by halfway was wheezing like a bellows. His father dragged his leg up step by step, and at the top wasn't even out of breath.

"You walk like you're chasing a hare," his father said, planting the hoe. "A hare can't run far; after a bit it lies down of itself, and so do you. Chasing a deer isn't like that. A deer walks steady, walks far, walks all day. Race it for speed and by noon you're lying down and it's still walking." He taught Xiaoman: three steps a breath in, three steps a breath out. Breathing in, the breath sinks down; breathing out, the feet go forward. Don't look at the top of the slope; look only at the step under your feet.

Xiaoman walked it once that way, and at the top really wasn't much out of breath. That night on the woodpile he moved the *three steps* into his belly: in, one-two-three; hold, count; out, one-two-three, out as steady as lifting a foot. The wild-goose down under his nose turned over, and didn't fly.

Fourth month, ninth. Man: sixty-seven. Feather turned over.

One month, up eleven. His father said, "Every road on the mountain gets walked like this."

Liu Douya had heard about the gate opening too. Every day he followed Xiaoman up to the slope field, learning three-steps-a-breath, learning it faster than anyone; at the top his face wasn't red and he wasn't panting. "Ninth of the ninth — I'm going with you." Old Liu heard from the edge of the field and rapped him on the backside with the hoe handle. "Go? Three days' road to the Si River — you going to eat the wind?" Liu Douya said nothing, and was back the next day as usual.

In the fifth month, before the new crop, Old Liu's rice jar hit bottom. Old Liu borrowed two pecks of rice from the Mas and put a red thumbprint on the note, at three percent a month. A He heard, did sums with her charcoal in a little blue-covered notebook for a long time, and when she'd done she looked at Liu Douya and said nothing.

At the end of the fifth month it rained seven days running. The basins in the corner went up to eighteen — the eighteenth was his mother's washbasin. On the seventh night the roof over the head of the kang opened up, and rain ran down the wall into the kang flue. Xiaoman dived to pull out the bamboo scroll; when he got it out it had soaked half the night in muddy water, the cords swollen. He held it and his hands went cold: ink meets water and not a word survives.

His mother lit the lamp and laid the slips out one by one on the stove to dry. Deep into the night she ran her fingers over them slip by slip, and at the last one looked up. "Not one character blurred." Mother and son sat facing the scroll a long time without a word. A bamboo scroll picked up in the mountains, cords half rotten, wormholes in the slips, soaked half a night in muddy water — and not one character blurred. His mother rolled it up and handed it to him, saying only: "Hide it somewhere else."

At the start of the sixth month the Mas' steward, Hu Si, came to Old Liu's to collect those two pecks of rice. The note said repay after the autumn; Hu Si scraped a fingernail over the words *after the autumn*. "The Mas' autumn is when the Mas say." Old Liu couldn't pay, so Hu Si named another price: "That ghost haunting the Shens' woodpile — send your Douya to take a good look at it. Look well, and the interest's halved."

That night Liu Douya crouched at the foot of the woodpile and didn't hide; he looked up and said softly, "Steward Hu sent me to look at the ghost." Xiaoman didn't answer. He finished that breath's count, let it all out, and only then took the old goose feather he no longer used from his jacket and tossed it down. "Take him this. Tell him the ghost holds its breath, and can't beat you — forty-four to thirty-seven." Liu Douya picked up the feather, stood a long while, and went.

Hu Si laughed over that feather a long time, and didn't take a single cash off the interest. But when the story reached Ma San's ears, Ma San didn't laugh. He tapped the table with his club and thought a while. "Holding his breath? The county posted a notice this spring. That Shen boy — he isn't thinking of sitting the immortal gate, is he?"

One hot night in the sixth month the three of them sat at the door in the cool. From the back hill came a howl, long and shrill, one after another, circling in the valley. Xiaoman jumped. "Wolves!" His father fanned himself and listened a while. "Wind."

Xiaoman didn't believe him. So his father put down the fan. "When your grandpa taught me listening, he told me a story first."

It was about a man called Ji Chang learning archery. His master told him first to learn not to blink; he lay under his wife's loom watching the treadle for two years, till an awl-tip at his eye wouldn't make him blink. Then his master told him to learn to see: he tied a louse with a hair from an ox's tail and hung it in the window and gazed at it every day, three years, till the louse looked as big as a cartwheel. Only then did he draw the bow, and one arrow went through the louse's heart, and the hair it hung from didn't break.

When he'd finished his father said, "An archer learns to look first. Us hunters, we learn to listen first. A wolf's howl is pushed out of a chest — warm; wind in a rock crack, however loud, is hollow. When you can't tell, shut your eyes. Your eyes will fool you; your ears won't."

Xiaoman shut his eyes and listened again. The howl went on, one after another, but he heard it: there was no breath taken in it. Anything alive calling that long has to take a breath; this sound took none. He opened his eyes. "It's hollow." His mother said beside him, "People, too." His father asked how people too. She said, "The loudest isn't always the real one. What makes no sound is what matters," and handed his father the bowl of cooled mung-bean soup.

That night on the woodpile, for the first time, Xiaoman shut his eyes and listened to himself. He heard it: breathing in, a *hiss* in his nose; breathing out, a *whoosh* from his mouth. The scroll said: in and out, let not your own ears hear. He'd practised nine months and all along been breathing as loud as wind in a rock crack.

So night after night he took that *hiss* and that *whoosh* and gathered them smaller, till only a thread was left, till even he couldn't hear it. The wild-goose down stopped flying, stopped turning over, and only trembled under his nose, again and again.

Sixth month, eleventh. Man: eighty-one. Feather trembled.

In the seventh month the count stuck at eighty-nine — stuck twenty-odd days, every line in his mother's accounts *eighty-nine*. One night he gritted his teeth and forced it up to ninety-one; the breath burst, the down flew again, and the next day he couldn't even reach eighty-nine.

Sitting on the woodpile, for the first time he thought: maybe a hundred and twenty was never meant for ordinary people to count. Old Zhou's little boy was a few months out of the womb; he himself was thirteen, counting the Chinese way.

exits.means: hesitates, decides not to go yet, waits

story.zh:
那天夜里，小满躺在炕上，对着黑暗，小声道：「不去……家里离不开我。再等三年。」

胸口的木牌，一下子凉了。那条亮了一整晚的尾巴，暗了下去——一明，一暗，一明——暗下去的那一下，比平时长。

他睁着眼睛躺到天亮。隔着一道布帘，他爹咳了半夜。
story.en:
That night Xiaoman lay on the kang and said softly into the dark: "I won't go… home can't do without me. Wait another three years."

The token at his chest went cold at once. The tail that had been lit all evening dimmed — bright, dim, bright — and the dim lasted longer than usual.

He lay with his eyes open till dawn. Through the cloth curtain his father coughed half the night.
